summary_html: Agency chooses **Differential Response (DR)**/**Alternative Response**: engage **services without court petition** when safety permits. FFPSA and IV-B/IV-E prevention funding support voluntary, front-end help to avert removals.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that the State's burden at a dispositional hearing on whether an appropriate treatment plan can be devised is preponderance of the evidence, and that proof of a single incident resulting in serious bodily injury to the child suffices to support a no-appropriate-treatment-plan finding without proof that the parent caused the injury.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the statutory circumstance in which the no-treatment-plan route displaces any service-based alternative response.
key_cases.quote: we conclude the district court erred by imposing a clear and convincing burden of proof on the state at the dispositional hearing.

key_cases.holding: As a matter of first impression the division held that the Americans with Disabilities Act does not pre-empt section 19-3-604(1)(b)(I), because the question whether reasonable accommodations could address a parent's mental impairment is subsumed within the statutory question whether an appropriate treatment plan can be devised.
key_cases.relevance: Where a parent's unfitness stems from mental impairment that no accommodation can address, the statute permits proceeding without the service-based route this node describes.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that it does not conflict with the ADA's requirement that a public entity make reasonable accommodations for qualified individuals with disabilities.

key_cases.holding: The division held that a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations for a parent's disability in deciding whether the treatment plan was appropriate and whether the department made reasonable efforts to rehabilitate the parent, and affirmed because the court had done so.
key_cases.relevance: Whether services can be delivered with accommodation bears directly on whether a family can be served without escalation.
key_cases.quote: a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations in deciding whether such a parent's treatment plan was appropriate and whether reasonable efforts were made to rehabilitate the parent.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the invalidation of a nonparental visitation order, holding that the Washington statute as applied violated the mother's due process right to make decisions concerning the care, custody and control of her children because the trial court gave no special weight to the presumption that a fit parent acts in her children's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: An alternative-response track that avoids a petition also avoids any adjudication of unfitness, so the agency's leverage over the family is bounded by the presumption the Court states here.
key_cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children
